title: "Consciousness is Brahman" — prajnanam brahma (3.1)
hook: the Aitareya ends by asking which one is the self, and answers with two words that became one of the great sayings
tomorrow: six students, one year of practice before asking

segments.voice: Yesterday: three births, in the father, from the mother, and in departing, and Vamadeva breaking out like a hawk. Today, the Aitareya's last chapter.

Point at yourself. Where did your finger go? Probably the chest, maybe the face. Now ask: is that me, or is that where I keep the thing that's me? It's a children's puzzle, and a very old one. The Aitareya saves it for its last chapter. After the worlds, the gods moving in, hunger and thirst, the door at the crown and the three births, it stops telling stories and asks straight out: who is this one we call the self? And it ends with two words.
screen: `POINT AT YOURSELF.` → `IS THAT ME?` → `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?`

segments.voice: First the question: is the self the one by which we see? By which we hear, smell, speak, taste? Then the text looks at the heart and mind and lists what they do. Awareness. Perception. Discernment. Intelligence. Wisdom. Insight. Steadiness. Thought. Reflection. Drive. Memory. Intention. Purpose. Life. Desire. Will. All of these, it says, are only names of prajnana. Prajnana means knowing, awareness, consciousness: pra, forth or fully, and jnana, knowing. Then the list widens. This is Brahman. This is Indra, and Prajapati, and all the gods. The five elements, earth, wind, space, water and fire. Every creature, born from an egg, a womb, moisture or a sprout. Horses, cows, people, elephants, whatever breathes, walks, flies or stands still. All of it is guided by consciousness, rests on consciousness. The world has consciousness for its eye. And then: prajnanam brahma. Consciousness is Brahman. Many Hindu teachers in the Advaita tradition count this among four mahavakyas, great sayings, one from each Veda. This is the Rig Veda's. You've already heard the other three this year: tat tvam asi in the Chandogya, and aham brahma asmi and ayam atma brahma in the Brihadaranyaka. Schools read the saying differently. Advaita hears a strict identity: awareness and Brahman are one. Other Vedanta schools hear Brahman as the conscious ground all knowing depends on, while keeping a distinction between the soul and God. Either way, the text points somewhere specific: not at the finger, but at what's aware of it.
screen: `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?` · `ALL THESE ARE NAMES OF PRAJNANA.` · `EVERYTHING RESTS ON CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `ONE OF FOUR GREAT SAYINGS.` · then, large: `PRAJNANAM BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: Notice seeing, even with your eyes closed, then hearing, then a thought passing, a memory, a small want. Each time, don't follow the thing; notice the knowing of it: seeing, known; sound, known; thought, known. Then, if you'd like, rest in the knowing itself, which doesn't need anything to hold.
Prajnana, knowing, awareness, consciousness. Prajnanam brahma: consciousness is Brahman, the Aitareya's closing word and, in the Advaita tradition, the great saying of the Rig Veda.
Your line: the great saying. Tomorrow, six students arrive with questions. Day four hundred four, done.

howItsDone: In the Advaita tradition, the four great sayings are taught to students and to those taking monastic vows, and prajnanam brahma is the one associated with the Rig Veda; teachers in other Vedanta schools comment on the same line differently.

fork.setup: the Aitareya asks: which one is the self? the one by which we see, hear, speak? what's its last answer?
fork.reveal: all the powers of heart and mind are names of prajnana; everything rests on it. prajnanam brahma: consciousness is Brahman.

original.note: Sanskrit prajñānaṃ brahma: pra, fully, + jñāna, knowing. Aitareya 3.1.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: consciousness is just the brain doing its work.
what it means: the Aitareya names every power of heart and mind as prajnana, and says consciousness is Brahman.
what a scholar hears: prajñāne pratiṣṭhitam, 'established in consciousness', and prajñā-netro lokaḥ, 'the world has consciousness for its eye', just before the saying (3.1.3).

chat.says: What does 'prajnanam brahma' mean? I keep hearing it.
options: Consciousness is Brahman; it's the Aitareya's great saying.
The wise one is Brahma, the god who creates the world.
Only the wisest people are allowed to speak of Brahman.
chat.meaning: After calling every power of the mind a name of prajnana, the Aitareya ends: prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman.
